blocks.text: A combination is a selection of elements from a set where, unlike a permutation, order does not matter. Choosing {1,2} is the same combination as choosing {2,1}, they are counted only once. This single distinction from permutations changes the shape of the entire search: instead of tracking which elements have been used anywhere in the array, combinations only need to track how far into the array the search has already progressed.

The number of ways to choose k elements from n is written C(n,k), read "n choose k", and computed as n! divided by (k! times (n-k)!). For n=4 and k=2, C(4,2) = 6, dramatically smaller than the 4! = 24 permutations of the same 4 elements, precisely because combinations do not count reorderings of the same set as distinct.

If your first instinct is "generate all permutations, then remove the reordered duplicates," that works but wastes enormous amounts of work. C(n,k) is typically far smaller than n!, and there is a direct way to enumerate combinations that never produces a duplicate in the first place.

The two counts are related directly: the number of k-element permutations of n items equals C(n,k) times k!, since every combination can itself be reordered k! ways. This relationship is a useful sanity check, for n=4, k=2: C(4,2) is 6, and 6 times 2! (which is 2) equals 12, matching the 12 ordered pairs you would get by choosing 2 elements from 4 where order does matter.

content.title: 1. Why a Start Index Replaces a Used Array

blocks.text: The key structural idea: instead of asking "which unused element should I place next" (the permutation question), combinations ask "which element, from this point in the array ONWARD, should I include next." By restricting every recursive call to only consider candidates at index start or later, and passing start+1 (or the current index +1) into the recursive call, the search structurally guarantees that no element already considered can ever be reconsidered in a different order.

This one design choice is what eliminates duplicates by construction rather than by cleanup: two different orderings of the same set, like choosing 1 then 2, versus choosing 2 then 1, simply cannot both occur, because once the search has moved past index of value 1, it can never come back to consider placing it after 2.
Pseudocode Skeleton
Tracing the search for all size-2 combinations from {1,2,3,4} shows the start index moving strictly forward at every level, never backward.

blocks.caption: At each level, the recursion only considers candidates from the current start index onward, so 2 is only ever paired with 1 by starting from index of 1, never the reverse.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762989-916185992.png

items: start=0: choose 1, partial=[1]. Recurse with start=1.
Unchoose 1. start=0: choose 2, partial=[2]. Recurse with start=2.
Record [2,3] and [2,4] the same way, then unchoose 2.
start=0: choose 3, partial=[3]. Recurse with start=3, record [3,4]. Unchoose 3.
start=0: choose 4, partial=[4]. Recurse with start=4, but start=4 has no candidates left (0 remaining, need 1 more), so this branch produces nothing.
Final result: [1,2], [1,3], [1,4], [2,3], [2,4], [3,4], exactly C(4,2) = 6 combinations, none repeated.

blocks.text: Notice the recursive call passes i + 1, not start + 1. This distinction matters: the loop variable i is the specific index just chosen, and the next recursive call must start immediately after IT, not after wherever the loop began. Passing start + 1 instead of i + 1 is a subtle but real bug that would skip candidates.

There are C(n,k) total combinations, and copying each one into the results list costs O(k), giving a time complexity of O(C(n,k) times k). The search space itself, before any pruning, is bounded by the number of nodes in the recursion tree, which is also proportional to C(n,k) once pruning (covered next) is applied.
Auxiliary space beyond the output is O(k) for the recursion depth, since the partial combination never exceeds size k before a value is recorded and the branch unwinds.

content.title: 5. Pruning: Stopping Branches That Cannot Succeed

blocks.text: A meaningful optimization: before exploring further from a given start index, check whether there are even enough remaining candidates to reach size k. If the partial combination currently has size current.size(), and needs k minus current.size() more elements, but only n minus start candidates remain from start to the end of the array, then whenever the remaining candidate count is less than what is still needed, this branch mathematically cannot succeed and can be abandoned immediately.

blocks.caption: When fewer candidates remain than are still needed, the branch is abandoned without ever recursing into it, unlike a branch with enough remaining candidates which continues normally.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762989-84044028.png
blocks.alt: Pruning: Stopping Branches That Cannot Succeed

blocks.text: This pruning does not change the asymptotic complexity in the worst case, but in practice it avoids a large number of recursive calls that would immediately fail the base case check, especially when k is close to n or the search is deep.

It is worth noting explicitly why this pruning is safe: the check only rules OUT branches that are guaranteed to fail, it never accidentally skips a branch that could have produced a valid combination. This distinguishes correct pruning from an incorrect early exit, which is a distinction worth being able to justify out loud in an interview whenever you add a pruning condition to a backtracking solution.

A closely related variant replaces the fixed size k with a target SUM: find all combinations of numbers that add up to a given target. The same start index technique applies, with two key differences worth contrasting directly against plain combinations.

blocks.text: The distinction of whether the next recursive call passes i or i + 1 is the entire difference between "candidates can repeat" and "candidates cannot repeat," and is one of the most common small details interviewers probe to check real understanding rather than memorized code.

content.title: 7. A Bitmask Alternative for Small n

blocks.text: When n is small (roughly n less than or equal to 20, so that an integer's bits can represent membership), combinations can also be enumerated without recursion at all, by iterating every integer from 0 up to (2^n minus 1) and checking which ones have exactly k bits set. Each such integer, read as a bitmask, directly encodes one combination: bit i set means element i is included.

This approach trades a clean O(C(n,k) times k) recursive search for a simpler but less efficient O(2^n times n) full scan over every possible subset, most of which get discarded by the popcount check. It is not the technique to lead with in an interview, the backtracking version above is both faster and demonstrates the more broadly reusable skill, but bitmask enumeration is a fast way to brute force small cases when writing a quick reference solution or verifying the backtracking version against.

Using a used boolean array like in permutations: this is unnecessary overhead for combinations and easy to get subtly wrong, since a used array does not, by itself, prevent generating the same set in a different order. The start index is both simpler and structurally correct.
Passing start + 1 instead of i + 1 into the recursive call: this silently restricts which elements are considered in ways that do not match the loop, sometimes skipping valid combinations.

Off by one errors in the pruning condition: the loop bound comparing i against nums.size() minus remainingNeeded is easy to get wrong in either direction, when in doubt, verify it against a small worked example like C(4,2) by hand before trusting it.
Combinations: the direct application, fixed size k, no repeats, no target sum.
Combination Sum: target sum instead of fixed size, candidates may be reused unlimited times, requiring the recursive call to pass i instead of i + 1.

Combination Sum II: target sum, but each candidate may be used at most once AND the input can contain duplicates, requiring both the i + 1 forward move and a duplicate skip condition similar to the one used in Permutations II.

Subsets: a close sibling that removes the size restriction entirely, every partial combination generated along the way (not just the ones reaching a fixed size k) is itself a valid answer, so results are recorded at every node of the recursion tree, not only at the leaves.
